# Intel® SGX SDK for Linux — Copilot instructions

These notes orient automated assistance and code review for this repository. They
are **guidance, not gates** — favor them, but use judgment, and never block a
contribution solely because a suggestion here isn't met.

## What this repository is

The Intel® Software Guard Extensions (Intel® SGX) SDK and enclave runtime for
Linux. It provides the trusted (in‑enclave) libraries, the untrusted host
libraries and runtime (`urts`, `enclave_common`), and the host tools
(`sgx_edger8r`, `sgx_sign`, `sgx_encrypt`). See [README.md](../README.md) for the
overview and [CONTRIBUTING.md](../CONTRIBUTING.md) for contribution rules.

Code splits into two trust domains; keep the distinction in mind when reviewing:

- **Trusted** — runs inside the enclave (e.g. `sdk/trts`, `sdk/tlibc`,
  `sdk/tlibcxx`, `sdk/tlibcrypto`, `sdk/tservice`, `sdk/tseal`). Treats all input
  crossing the boundary as untrusted, and must be tight.
- **Untrusted** — host‑side code (`enclave_runtime/urts`,
  `enclave_runtime/enclave_common`, untrusted helpers, tools, samples). More room
  for manoeuvre than trusted code, but still security‑relevant.

The trusted/untrusted boundary is declared in **EDL** (`.edl`) files and the C
stubs are generated by `sgx_edger8r`.

The code is coupled, but roughly: `enclave_runtime` (plus parts of `common`) is
the **leaf** of the dependency tree, and `sdk` loosely builds on top. The SDK is
largely independent, but uses `urts` for its simulation capability. When a
component has its own `README.md`, defer to it for the authoritative detail.

This repository is vendored into the consolidated Intel® SGX for Linux distribution
at https://github.com/intel/confidential-computing.sgx, and components of it are also
used by https://github.com/intel/confidential-computing.tee.dcap — consult those for
the big‑picture, cross‑component context. This SDK is also what Intel uses to build
the Architecture Enclaves (prebuilt, signed by Intel) shipped with the Intel® SGX
Platform Software (PSW).

## Repository layout

- `sdk/` — SDK trusted/untrusted libraries and host tools.
- `enclave_runtime/` — untrusted runtime (`urts`) and enclave‑common loader.
- `common/` — shared headers (`common/inc/` public, `common/inc/internal/`
  internal) and support code.
- `SampleCode/` — sample enclaves and host apps.
- `external/` — third‑party dependencies, vendored as submodules.
- `build_infrastructure/` — packaging, installer, container, and reproducible‑build
  tooling.

## Building and testing

A real build needs the prerequisites listed in [README.md](../README.md). The
common SDK build flow (for the runtime part, see
[enclave_runtime/README.md](../enclave_runtime/README.md)) is:
```bash
make preparation        # init submodules, apply patches, fetch prebuilt deps — run first
make sdk                # build the SDK (default target)
make sdk_install_pkg    # produce the self-extracting installer (.bin)
```

- `make preparation` is required before any build; it initializes submodules and
  prepares `external/`.
- Simulation mode (`SGX_MODE=SIM`) builds and runs without SGX hardware but offers
  **no** security guarantees — it's for development and CI smoke tests only.
- Build flavors: `USE_OPT_LIBS` selects the crypto backend (Intel IPP by default;
  the OpenSSL‑based SGXSSL path is legacy). The SDK also builds in several
  CVE‑2020‑0551 mitigation flavors. See the build instructions for details.
- Samples build against an installed SDK after `source <sdk>/environment`; a
  sample's `make && make run` is the quickest end‑to‑end smoke test. `SGX_MODE=SIM`
  exercises the flow without SGX hardware — hardware‑only paths can't be covered in
  a hardware‑less CI.

The headline release artifact is the self‑extracting **`.bin` SDK installer** (the
untrusted runtime additionally ships as distro packages — you need the SDK to build
an enclave and the runtime to run one). CI builds the installer on push and pull
request; CI artifacts are non‑production and exist only to validate the build.
By default the build produces the installer using a pre‑built Intel IPP crypto
library downloaded from https://download.01.org/intel-sgx/ (Intel's publishing
venue for Intel® SGX, as noted in the README); it can also be configured to use the
OpenSSL‑based SGXSSL path, or to compile IPP crypto from source (e.g. for
reproducibility or to refresh the prebuilt).

## Contribution conventions

Follow [CONTRIBUTING.md](../CONTRIBUTING.md). In short:

- A PR should have a **single clear purpose**; keep commits small and atomic and
  squash fixups so merged history stays clean.
- **Every commit must be signed off** (DCO): `Signed-off-by: Name <email>` —
  `git commit -s`. Use a known identity.
- Match the **existing style** of the file you're editing; keep the license/
  copyright header intact on every source file. When you touch a file whose header
  still carries the full license text, consider migrating it to the short
  `SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause` form (other headers already use it), and
  keep the copyright line accurate for your contribution.
- Explain anything non‑obvious in comments, the commit message, or the PR
  description.
- **Follow responsible disclosure for security issues.** This is a widely‑deployed
  security product, so a vulnerability landing unscrutinised (without review and a
  fix ready) would put downstream users at risk — don't describe a suspected
  vulnerability in a public issue or PR; follow [SECURITY.md](../SECURITY.md).

For deeper or repository‑specific guidance, you may also consult any `README*/*`
branches in this repository (if present) and a component's own `README.md`.

## Code review

Keep automated review constructive and welcoming to new contributors. Frame
findings as suggestions with a brief rationale, prioritize correctness and
security of the trusted/untrusted boundary, and avoid nitpicking style that
already matches surrounding code. Beyond that:

- **Security first.** This is a security‑sensitive project: hold memory safety,
  defensive coding, and secure‑coding practices to a high bar — especially in
  trusted (in‑enclave) code.
- **Mind backward compatibility.** This is a mature, long‑lived project with many
  legacy callers. External interfaces should stay backward compatible and C‑ABI
  stable. API breaks are sometimes necessary but must be clearly documented; if a
  PR already calls a break out, flag it for reviewer attention and try to gauge the
  impact — but if it's already properly explained and analyzed, move on.
- **Suggest modern improvements, don't insist.** Some code predates modern C++ and
  is C‑like. It's fine — encouraged — to propose safer, more modern constructs
  (especially during refactors), but don't be blocked by surrounding code being
  dated, and expect that the author may reasonably decline. Target **C++17** for
  the SDK's own code; the supported toolchains go back to older distributions (see
  the README's supported‑OS list, as old as Debian 10 at the time of this writing). A *downstream consumer* may
  compile the shipped headers at a newer standard, so those headers should still
  compile cleanly and degrade feature use gracefully.
- **Internally modern, externally C.** Prefer modern, memory‑safe C++ in
  implementation; expose a portable C ABI at the boundary. The SDK is consumed from
  C, C++, and Rust (via FFI), and should remain consumable from other languages
  (e.g. Python, Java). This repository does not ship language wrappers of its own.
